utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-06-90-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This session this afternoon, let me explain that I am presiding today simply because I am Pre-Trial Judge. Today's session is at the instance of General Gotovina's Defence team, who asked to be given an opportunity to give oral argument in addition to or to supplement their written motion on the question of jurisdiction. May we hear the team, please -- before that, can we get the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good afternoon. On behalf of General Gotovina, Greg Kehoe, Luka Misetic, and Professor Payam Akhavan, and assisting behind Professor Akhavan is Jelena Madunic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Laurel Baig, Michelle Jarvis for the Prosecution, assisted by case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any appearances for Mr. Cermak? Any appearances for Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good day. I am Miroslav Separovic, Attorney-at-law, and together with us is Goran Mikulicic and our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I see there is an accused in the court. Is that Mr. Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: General Gotovina, can you hear me in the language you understand? THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, if we ought to -- I assume Your Honour wants to commence discussion on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would like to turn it over to Professor Akhavan for the presentation of on the behalf of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Professor Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. President, distinguished members of the Tribunal. It is an honour and privilege to appear before you today on behalf of General Gotovina. The essential argument of our motion is very simple. The Prosecution cannot accuse General Gotovina of crimes against humanity while disregarding the laws of war. The Prosecution cannot ask the Tribunal to re-write customary law, to compensate for the inadequacies of its case. Having initially argued that the laws of war are inapplicable, the Prosecution's second response now argues that humanitarian law is applicable but only to a limited extent. But the Prosecution, once again, completely disregards contrary ICTY jurisprudence and its own contrary legal position prior to this case. The Prosecution's core theory in the indictment is that General Gotovina was part of a joint criminal enterprise to ethnically cleanse Krajina Serbs through mass deportation. This deportation campaign was allegedly executed in two phases, before and after the restoration of Croatian state authority over the Krajina. It is alleged that during Operation Storm psychological warfare and the shelling of civilians resulted in the mass exodus of Serbian civilians. It is further alleged that upon successful conclusion of Operation Storm and the collapse of the Republika Srpska Krajina, the return of civilians was discouraged through Croatian colonisation and the destruction or pillage of Serbian property. It is also asserted that General Gotovina is liable for murder and cruel treatment merely because such crimes were a possible consequence of the joint criminal enterprise, even if they were not subjectively predictable to him. The fundamental flaw of this theory is that the Prosecution unilaterally eliminates an essential element of deportation as defined by Article 49 of the 4th Geneva Convention. The indictment does not state anywhere that the alleged victims of deportation were in the hands of Croatian forces in territory under Croatian control. The Prosecution's second response openly argues that this argument of Article 49 is inapplicable to crime against humanity and that alleged shelling of civilian areas was a modality of deportation. If the Prosecution is correct, the Tribunal has jurisdiction over the indictments; but if the Prosecution is not correct, its entire ethnic cleansing case falls apart because there can be no joint criminal enterprise if the alleged acts simply do not constitute the crime of deportation. The Prosecution's submissions completely disregard ICTY jurisprudence, humanitarian law, and the Prosecution's own earlier position on this issue. The Stakic appeal's judgement recognise that Article 49 is "the underlying instrument prohibiting deportation."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please show down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, you are asked to please slow down. Apparently, you are little too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I understand. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask you to please stick to what is not already in the papers, because so far you have told us what you have already told us in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. I will be elaborating on what we have already included in our written pleadings and will not burden you by repeating what is already there. I've indicated earlier that the Stakic appeals judgement clearly indicates that there is a requirement of occupied territory. I would wish to add that in the more recent Naletilic appeals judgement, Judge Schomburg expressly stated, and this is at page 225, paragraph 22, that under Article 5 deportation must be "from an area under the actual control of one village or party to an area under the actual control of another." If the alleged victims of deportation were never in the hands of Croatian forces, the crime of deportation was simply never committed. The argument that the occupation requirement of Article 49 does not apply to deportation does not find support in any of the authorities cited by the Prosecution, but what is most remarkable is that prior to this case the Prosecution itself has consistently and repeatedly maintained that this element of Article 49 does apply to the crime against humanity of deportation. To give one example in the Simic pre-trial brief at paragraph 97, relying on the Krnojelac trial judgement, the Prosecution categorically stated that: "The content of the underlying offence of deportation does not differ whether perpetrated as a war crime or as a crime against humanity."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: "The crime against humanity" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: My Apologies. Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one thing in addition. You are quoting a lot of cases. Could you please always indicate when you're talking about deportation or forcible removal, whether you're quoting from a crimes against humanity case or a war crimes case so that we can clearly distinguish between the two types of crimes charged in the cases you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, Judge Orie. Many apologies. It's been some years since I stood in this Chamber, and I'm not yet advanced enough with the technology. Apologies. Judge Orie, just to re-affirm that the quotation from the Simic pre-trial brief specifically speaks about crimes against humanity under Article 5(D), and as I mentioned the Prosecution categorically states in their pre-trial brief: "As a crime against humanity, deportation requires proof of the same elements as that required under Article 49 for war crimes." Another example is the Kovacevic pre-trial brief at page 32 where the Prosecutor stated that: "Deportation under Article 5 reflects the same actions as those in Article 49 of Geneva Convention 4." The Prosecutor recognises that certain requirements of nationality, for instance, under Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions may not apply, but that is totally irrelevant with the issue that is before us today. So we have to ask, Mr. President, why is the Prosecutor suddenly disavowing its own earlier position. Why is the Prosecution seeking an exception specifically in the case of General Gotovina? We submit respectfully that the Gotovina exception is an attempt by the Prosecution to criminalise Operation Storm without proof that it constituted unlawful combat, if alleged that the purpose of Operation Storm was terrorisation and mass expulsion of civilians because there was no legitimate military objective. But the Prosecution does not explain why five and a half years after the initial indictment against General Gotovina, the defendant has not been properly charged with unlawful attacks or spreading terror, which are the appropriate crimes. Now that the indictment's profound legal flaw has been exposed, the Prosecution tells us in its recent response that it is prepared to add further counts of Hague law violations; this with just two months before the trial begins. The Prosecution's theory on post-combat second phase of ethnic cleansing is equally problematic. The allegation is that Croatian colonisation and destruction or pillage of property after the conclusion of Operation Storm amounts to deportation because it discouraged the return of Serbs. This is a highly imaginative theory but the Prosecution cannot retroactively consummate the crime of deportation when Croatian forces never deported protected persons from occupied territory in the first place. The mere impact of the alleged wanton destruction or plunder cannot transform those crimes into the substantively different crime of deportation. Another fundamental flaw is the allegation of post-debellatio war crimes. The only armed conflict alleged in the indictment is "in the Krajina region of the Republic of Croatia," which is defined elsewhere in the indictment as UN protected area sectors north and south. It's further admitted in the indictment that by 7 August 1995 minimal or non-existent Serbian resistance was completely overcome. The Prosecution's latest response --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: It is further admitted that by 7 August non-existent or minimal Serbian resistance was completely overcome.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel also speak into the microphone, please, and slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, you will remember that you've got ten minutes to speak from the time you started in terms of the decision that granted the permission. You're very close to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I planned on ten minutes not including the interruptions, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I crave your indulgence. The Prosecution's latest response now alleges for the first time ever that an armed conflict continued to exist post-debellatio simply because the Dayton and Erdut peace agreements were not yet concluded. But debellatio does not depend on formal agreements, whether an armistice or capitulation. The Prosecution's new argument is legally irrelevant and effectively concedes that there was no armed conflict in the Krajina. It is also an attempt to effectively amend the indictment by introducing a wholly new legal theory, again with just two months before the trial begins. If the proper law of deportation and debellatio is applied nothing is left of the case against General Gotovina. Rarely, if ever, has an indictment been so deeply flawed, so manifestly inconsistent with customary law, and we respectfully submit that under the circumstances subjecting General Gotovina to a trial would be a miscarriage of justice. Mr. President, we must also consider the far-reaching implications of this motion on the Tribunal's legacy as it enters its final months. There comes a point at which expansion of humanitarian law begins to resemble a legal utopia, rather than realistic rules that can be followed by military commanders acting in good faith. Mr. President, distinguished members of the Tribunal, in concluding, I note that we've come a long way since the historic Tadic jurisdiction motion when seminal issues of humanitarian law remained to be elucidated. But 14 years after the Tribunal's establishment, we're once again faced with fundamental questions of jurisdiction reminiscent of the early days of Tadic. Today's proceeding may well be the historic response to Tadic. A final opportunity for this Tribunal to send a message that just as it once expanded humanitarian law, it will now draw the line and not allow military commanders to be subjected to prosecution, unless it is properly alleged that they have violated humanitarian law. That concludes, Mr. President, our brief submission. I thank the Chamber for its patience and remain at your disposal for questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please switch off his microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of the Defence of General Markac, my co-counsel, Mr. Goran Mikulicic will address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is a pleasure to point out some arguments which accompany our written submissions, challenging the jurisdiction of this Tribunal in relation to the indictment as it was legally formulated by the Prosecution in this case. In order to avoid any repetition, either in relation to what was stated in our written submissions or in relation to what was just said by my friend of from the Defence of General Gotovina, please allow me to say that the Defence of General Markac fully supports and accepts the arguments of General Gotovina in relation to the existence of an armed conflict and deportation of the population. In addition to that I would like to point out the well-known legal principle beneficium cohesiones, which is a legal principle stating that what is in favour of one accused should be applied to other accused in the same proceedings as well. What is stated or what is the position of General Markac's Defence is that in the relevant period of time and in any case in the time before the beginning of the Operation Storm and immediately after its conclusion, in the theatre of alleged crimes in the territory of the so-called Sector South of the self-proclaimed Republic of Krajina, there was no armed conflict. This position of the Defence is based on the arguments which we articulated in writing. Now, we would just like to add a couple of words to that. In their response, my learned friends from the Prosecution point out that in our motion challenging the jurisdiction, we are actually dealing with a so-called factual issue; namely, that the existence of an armed conflict is a quaestio facti, a factual question that needs to be litigated. This claim is only partially correct because the issue of whether an armed conflict existed or not is also a legal issue, which is very important for these proceedings, or rather, it is so important that it actually defines the jurisdiction ratione materiae or subject matter jurisdiction of this Tribunal. The factual issue can be analysed only on the basis of a criterium which was used by Pre-Trial Judges who confirmed the indictment, or rather, in this situation when the indictment is expanded and this criterium is a so-called prima facie criterium. It is our position that by applying prima facie criterium, given the documentation supporting the indictment and provided by the Prosecution, a conclusion cannot be drawn that during the relevant period of time there was a conflict between regular forces of the Republic of Croatia and armed forces of the self-proclaimed Republic of Serbian Krajina. We base this conclusion, first and foremost, on the document which accompanied our written submissions which is a report of Secretary-General of the UN about the events in Sector South on the date of -- or during the period leading up to the 20th of August, 1995. In that report it is explicitly stated that following the launch of the military and police Operation Storm in which military and police forces of the Republic of Croatia participated, there followed an exodus and fleeing of the political and other leadership of the self-proclaimed Serbian Republic of Krajina. Another document from the supporting material indicates that the entire 21st Corps of the army of the self-proclaimed Serbian Republic of Krajina surrendered. This leads us to the following conclusion. First, that any further armed activity in that area transpired in the circumstances where there was no organisation and no intensity. No organisation because, based on the documents, it is clear that political and military leadership had left the area, so there was nobody else there to organise the armed rebellion. And as for the lack of intensity, it is based on the fact that a very large number of the soldiers of the self-proclaimed army actually surrendered to the Croatian forces. I insist on these two terms; namely, organisation and intensity, because on the basis of the humanitarian law as it exists so far, these two are the elements which are included in the legal qualification of an armed conflict, and they are also very important in the distinction between the qualification of an armed conflict and the so-called internal tensions and unrest. In addition to this we pointed out to many portions of the case law, both of this Tribunal and that of Rwanda, and we also highlighted comments of the International Red Cross which accompany the Geneva Conventions and which altogether form customary international law. Distinction between the existence of an armed conflict and internal tensions and unrest lies precisely in these two key terms, which are the organisation of unrest and the question of intensity of activities. In both cases, these two criteria coincide based on the supporting material. It is our position that by applying a prima facie test, one can only come to the conclusion that the Prosecution failed to prove their allegation that throughout the entire time, to which the indictment refers, there existed a state of armed conflict in the Serbian Republic of Krajina. And if there was no state of armed conflict under -- during which crimes were committed, then this Chamber has no jurisdiction to decide in this case. We pointed this out and supported this with case law, saying that the application of Article 3 and 5 of this Tribunal can only be valid when there is a state of an armed conflict, be it an international one or an internal one. And to conclude, we remain firm in the arguments presented in our written submissions, stating that the supporting material contains such documents that greatly challenge the formulation of the indictment when it comes to the state of armed conflict. Based on that, we believe that such an indictment containing such legal qualifications should not have been confirmed and that in that respect, this Honourable Chamber should reject such an indictment. I am at your disposal for any questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, although any of the three of us may be available for questions should the Bench have some of the Prosecution, Ms. Baig will be presenting the submissions on behalf of the Prosecution, and I yield the floor to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only issue before this Trial Chamber is whether the Tribunal has jurisdiction over the crimes charged in the indictment. Jurisdiction means that the Tribunal has the power to prosecute the crimes charged. Factual disputes and the precise contours of the legal definitions of the crimes are not matters that go to jurisdiction and should be addressed on the basis of the arguments and the evidence at trial. The indictment charges persons covered by the statute with violations of Articles 3 and 5 within the time and region set out in the Statute. Thus, the Defence arguments fall outside of the narrow definition of jurisdiction set out in Article 72(D). For example, disputes about the existence, duration, intensity of the armed conflict are purely questions of fact. These must be determined on the basis of the evidence adduced at the trial. Likewise, the erroneous assumption that the attacks on civilians were lawful rests on a factual dispute. The Prosecution alleges that the accused unlawfully attacked civilians, civilian areas, and civilian convoys in order to drive the civilians from the RSK. This is prohibited under international humanitarian law. It also constitutes a crime against humanity. The fact that the Prosecutor has not charged the shelling, for example, as a separate war crime does not mean that the acts were legal. Whether or not the shelling caused deportation, forcible transfer, or formed part of a persecutory campaign is a matter of fact which must be determined at the trial on the basis of the evidence presented. It is not a question of jurisdiction. The Defence attempt to characterise the shelling of civilians as "legal," according to the laws or customs of war, allows it to set up a false conflict between international humanitarian law and crimes against humanity which does not actually exist in this case. IHL and crimes against humanity operate harmoniously. The definition of the crimes against humanity adopted in the case law already incorporates the realities of war and accepts that there may be attacks which are not directed at the civilian population and that there may be military reasons justifying deportation which exclude criminal responsibility for crimes against humanity. The Defence arguments do not raise jurisdictional issues and this should dispose of the matter. Moreover, the Appeals Chamber's jurisprudence has already defined the elements of the crimes of deportation, forcible transfer, and crimes -- and persecution as crimes against humanity. The definition does not include any of the new elements advanced by the Defence. In Stakic, for example, the Appeals Chamber defined the actus reus of deportation as: "The forced displacement of persons by expulsion or other forms of coercion from the area in which they are lawfully present, across a de jure state border, or, in certain circumstances, a de facto border, without grounds permitted under international law." That's the crimes against humanity deportation definition. It is incorrect to say that crimes against humanity of deportation and forcible transfer can only be committed through the ordering mode of liability in internal conflicts. The Appeals Chamber convicted Stakic of JCE liability and not for ordering the crime of deportation. At least five other cases of this Tribunal have convicted for deportation as a crime against humanity for modes of liability other than ordering: Simic, Krnojelac, Kupreskic, Brdjanin, and Blagojevic. Second, it is incorrect that deportation and other crimes against humanity cannot be committed through any of the modalities of war. In this case, that the shelling cannot form part of the actus reus of the crime against humanity. In Stakic, Blagojevic, Brdjanin, the deportation was conducted, at least in part, through fear instilled by shelling. Employing the Defence terminology, the accused committed a Geneva law violation through a Hague law violation. Thirdly, crimes against humanity are not limited to situations akin to occupation. No ICTY case has ever required this novel element for crimes against humanity. Even in international humanitarian law, occupation or its equivalent is not required for the crime of forced displacement in internal armed conflict. The Defence's attempting to import the special requirements of Article 49 of Geneva Convention 4 into Article 17 of Additional Protocol II. This is contrary to the express statement in Article 2 of Additional Protocol II that the scope of the Protocol extends to "all persons affected by the armed conflict." The logic of the Defence's new elements - that Article 5 must be determined and defined wholly by reference to IHL - rests on an incomplete and inaccurate understanding of the principle of lex specialis. Lex specialis does not mean that anything not specifically prohibited by IHL is specifically allowed during war. The principle means that other bodies of law should not be interpreted in a way that undermines IHL during armed conflict. But this does not exclude the concurrent application of other bodies of law. Where there are silences in IHL, where IHL does not specifically provide for the situation, then other law can fill these gaps to ensure the protection of victims to the conflict. The argument that international humanitarian law applies to the exclusion of every other law in armed conflict is simply wrong. International humanitarian law is full of reminders that other principles continue to apply to supplement its protection. The Martens Clause in the Preamble of The Hague Regulations of 1907 is an excellent example of IHL recognising the importance of the laws of humanity. This is also picked up in the Preamble to Additional Protocol II. The co-existence of the two bodies of law was expressly recognised in the Nuremberg Charter which introduces crimes against humanity in connection with the armed conflict. The importance of this was recognised in the Justice case, where the Chamber acknowledged that the similar provision in of Control Counsel Law 10 were not surplusage. They supplemented the preceding sections on war crimes and prohibited atrocities "against any civilian population." The ICTY Statute itself is clear that crimes against humanity can be committed during armed conflict. The definition of deportation itself takes into account the military realities that govern the law -- that are governed by the law of armed conflict. In deportation the only thing that's prohibited by the crime against humanity definition is forced displacement without grounds permitted under international law. The reality of war is built into that definition. Lex specialis does not mean that the operation of crimes -- that the operation of crimes against humanity is excluded in armed conflict. It does not mean that the elements of crimes against humanity must match the elements of war crimes. Limiting Article 5, Crimes of Deportation and Forcible Transfer, to the same subset of situations that's already covered by international humanitarian law would undermine the rationale for the development of crimes against humanity, to extend the reach of international criminal law beyond the restricted category of persons protected by international humanitarian law, and, in particular at the time of the Second World War, to cover crimes committed by a party to the conflict against its own nationals. The Defence argument seeks to reverse this development. What the principle of lex specialis demands and what the Tribunal has already delivered is that crimes against humanity have to be interpreted in a manner that respects the lex specialis of international humanitarian law. Accepting the argument that the two sets of crimes must necessarily be identical would render crimes against humanity redundant in armed conflict. Thank you, subject to any questions that you might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a -- one or more questions. Mr. Akhavan, you said it's further alleged that upon successful conclusion of Operation Storm, the collapse of the Republika Srpska Krajina, the return of civilians was discouraged through Croatian colonisation and the destruction or pillage of property. From what I remember, the Prosecution strongly disagrees that this is alleged. Of course, the Prosecution has drafted the indictment. Could you tell me exactly, in order to better understand your disagreement, where I find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I draw your attention to paragraph 36 of the indictment. The Prosecution there asserts: "A demographic policy was also implemented." So they're arguing on the one hand that the shelling caused the mass exodus of civilians; and then after Croatia captures the territory, there's a demographic policy whereby much of the Serb Krajina was to be colonized with Croats, whereby Croatian forces and other Croats were moved into many of these abandoned Serb houses that survived. Homes belonging to Serbs were expropriated. While rights to return to the area or reclaimed property may have formerly existed, the destruction of Serb property and their papers under the circumstances of mass flight made such relief largely artificial and unavailable and intentionally so." We have argued that the crime under Article 49, paragraph 6 of the 4th Geneva Convention of transferring by a state of its own population into territory occupied by another state clearly does not apply to internal armed conflict. This is reflected in Rule 130 of the ICRC study on customary law. Now, the Prosecution's response concedes that they are not charging this crime. They are not charging the crime of colonisation; that is an admission by the Prosecution in its latest response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: But what they are saying is that they will use this action as a means of inferring a persecutory intent and the intent to deport by making the displacement of the Serbian population permanent. What we would respectfully submit that if you're not charging this conduct as a crime, if indeed it is not a crime under humanitarian law, then one cannot even begin to draw adverse circumstances, adverse inferences of intention. And we've pointed in our submission that we have no intention to dispute questions of fact, and our colleague is entirely correct. We are only concerned with the Tribunal's jurisdiction. But we need to note that in the Martic case in the other cases dealing with this, the Prosecution itself has acknowledged that almost 100.000 Croats were ethnically cleansed from the Krajina. So to turn around now and say that the return or the re-settlement of those people is either a crime under humanitarian law formally or if it's not charged as a crime will now be a basis for making an allegation of Croatian colonisation, which is a very serious allegation, we respectfully say would be beyond the Tribunal's jurisdiction because it does not conform with the customary law and it constitutes retroactive criminalisation of otherwise lawful conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please forgive me. I understood the indictment to say that, and I'm looking, for example, at paragraph 50, that what the accused are charged with is "the execution of the forcible transfer and/or deportation of members of the Krajina Serb population from the southern portion of the Krajina region;" and then a few other areas are mentioned "by the threat and/or commission of a violent and intimidating acts." That's the crime charged if I understand well; whereas, in paragraph 36, but please correct me when I read this wrong, that as one of the factual circumstances it is set out that Croats were then moved into abandoned Serb houses, which is dramatically enough that they may have been removed from the houses at an earlier stage. But let's just for argument's sake, let's assume that you're right, that Serbs are moved and Croatians were removed from a certain area. Now, if that territory is re-gained by Croatian forces, and let's just assume - and that's what I read in the indictment - that then the Serbs who earlier moved in -- when this territory is re-gained are -- is it allowed in your view or is it a crime that you remove then the civilian population, because you say something about the return of civilians was discouraged through Croatian colonisation; whereas, I read that they were just removed from that territory. Would that change anything in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I should clarify our position. Our position is that the crime of -- under Article 49, paragraph 6 of the 4th Geneva Convention is that of colonisation or imposition of settlements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not charged, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No, it's not. The Prosecution has now clarified that that was not charged. It was not clear from the initial indictment, because the word "to colonize" has a certain meaning in humanitarian law. If you're accusing -- if you're accusing Croatia of colonizing its own territory, there is a problem. We would submit there is a problem. Now, the point we are making is that on the one hand the Prosecution alleges that the mass expulsion of Serbs was achieved primarily through the conduct of hostilities, through shelling of civilians; then the Croatian forces arrived. The vast majority of Serbs have already left; then the allegation is that because of wanton destruction and pillage, there is a policy to prevent the return of those who already left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How could we then read, if you allow me to interrupt, whether true or not, that's of course a matter of evidence, that's not what Article 50 says, isn't it? It doesn't say that those who were already -- had already left, but it's about the forcible transfer and deportation of members of the Krajina Serbs. It doesn't say anything about discouraging return. So I wonder --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Those paragraphs are incorporated by reference in Article -- in paragraph 50. Paragraph 50 says that: "Acts alleged in paragraphs 12 to 21 and 28 to 47 are included." So they are including in their deportation count the alleged colonisation of the Krajina as a factor establishing deportation. Now, we submit that, first, you must consummate the crime of deportation. If Article 49 of the conventions, if this Tribunal's case law, if the Prosecution's own submissions in its own pre-trial briefs expressly recognises a requirement that the victims being the hands of a party to the conflict, then they have not satisfied that element. There is no crime of deportation. You cannot retroactively consummate the crime of deportation when an essential element never existed. And to suggest also, in addition to that fact, that colonisation is a basis for arriving at that conclusion, we would say is problematic because that is not a crime under humanitarian law. They've said that they're not charging that as a crime, but they're still going to use it as a means of inferring a relative intent. And that we think is also problematic, in addition to the legal issue, which we raised in our earlier submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now better understand the way you interpret the indictment, which certainly assists me in better understanding your argument. One of the arguments that has been raised is by charging crimes against humanity under Article 5, you deprive the accused from the defence that what actually was done was lawful warfare. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No, I would clarify that, and with due respect, I think that was a mischaracterisation for argument. We are not suggesting that you cannot charge unlawful attacks as crimes against humanity. This is very clearly possible under the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. The Galic case is a perfect example where conduct of hostilities was charged against crimes against humanity, and we think that it would be totally unacceptable to create such a gap in humanitarian law; whereby, people could be victimised through indiscriminate shelling, for example, and you could not charge it. That's not what we're saying. What we're saying is very simple. We are saying you have to satisfy the elements of the crime; that's all we're saying. And the crime of deportation is not the proper charge in this case. Now, why would the Prosecution charge shelling -- alleged shelling of civilians as deportation as opposed to other crimes which are equally possible within crimes against humanity. You have the crime of murder which was charged in Galic, and in Galic they said that the underlying offence of murder is the same for Article 5 as it is for Article 3. And the Prosecution says that if we don't apply the laws of war to charging crimes against humanity lawful combat would be impossible. That is in the submission of the Prosecution. So all we're saying is you cannot charge shelling as Article 5 and avoid proof of the elements of the crime of deportation, and also avoid proof that these acts were actually unlawful. And if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me try to understand you. If you charge a crime against humanity, you'll have to prove whether the Prosecution is in a position to do so, yes or no, I don't know. But you have to prove that the crime was committed in a widespread and/or systematic attack against civilians. What -- how could the laws of war provide for a justification or an excuse for a widespread and/or systematic attack against civilians? I'm trying to understand what I at least thought your argument was.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No. It certainly -- most certainly is not, and I regret if I've given that impression. We categorically would not make such an argument. Crimes against humanity has mens rea requirement, knowledge of broader context of widespread and systematic attack, and it has an actus reus requirement, in this case deportation. There are two levels of analysis. One is what is the crime of deportation, which needs to be proved in order then to link it with the mens rea of knowledge of a widespread or systematic attack. The crime of deportation involves the forcible expulsion of those who are in the hands of a party to the conflict. We would submit there's no doubt about that. If you do not prove the underlying crime of deportation, then the mens rea of crimes against humanity is not consummated. There is no crime. Now, even with respect to knowledge of the context, you cannot use an otherwise lawful act to infer criminal intent if you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lawful act. Which lawful act do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, for instance, if it is the case that there are lawful military targets in Knin and there is a lawful attack in order to take out those military targets, in the course of shelling, civilians flee as they always do in situations of combat in every warfare that one can -- act of warfare that one can think about, the mere fact that civilians have fled is not a war crime or a crime against humanity, nor can it be a basis for inferring criminal intent on the part of the accused. You must establish that the attacks either deliberately targeted civilians or that they were indiscriminate attacks or disproportionate attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there, because that's exactly what I would like to clarify with you. What you say is if you target a military attack, civilians might flee, they might be, if they are killed, could be collateral damage of this. You say if there is a lawful military target, I think you say it's wrong to charge under Article 5 because that could be the case. Could you explain to me, how could you possibly prove that the act was part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians, where at the same time later in your argument you say: Well, it could well be that it was a military target, a justified military target, and it was collateral damage. Attacking a military target and having collateral damage among civilians, how is that to be reconciled with, let's just assume, a proven widespread or systematic attack against civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Indeed. In order to prove a widespread or systematic attack, you have to establish that there were criminal acts. If you establish merely that there were unfortunate circumstances of wartime, war is brutal, it is tragic, it is unfortunate in the sense that every war has victims when civilians flee, when there is collateral damage, it doesn't change anything whether we're talking about the NATO bombardment of Kosovo or if we're talking about Operation Storm. But the mere fact that there was civilian casualties or in this case civilians who flee does not establish a widespread and systematic attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean that if in the situation you are depicting, the situation being something that there is collateral damage when a military target is attacked; that if that's the case, and that's of course a matter of facts that happened, then there would be an acquittal almost automatically under Article 5 because the widespread and systematic attack could not be proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: As a matter of fact yes, but we are raising here a point of law. The point of law is that the circumstances where there's occupation under the Geneva law is a totally different body of law compared to The Hague law where there is no occupation. The main difference is when someone is in your hands, there's an absolute prohibition against inhumane treatment. If someone is a prisoner of war or civilian occupied territory, they cannot be harmed in any way. But in the conduct of hostilities, as we know from the Prosecutor's own NATO report, 500 civilians were killed in NATO's bombardment of Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all facts. I don't know yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: This is what we've submitted. It's in the report of the Prosecution. The Prosecution establishes 500 people were killed, a thousand were injured, but decides not to charge anyone with war crimes or crimes against humanity. Why? Because there is no widespread or systematic attack within the meaning of crimes against humanity, even though 500 people are killed and a thousand are injured. We submit here you cannot simply say there was shelling of civilians, a lot of people left, that is a crime against humanity of deportation, but we're not going to prove the elements of The Hague law, which prove this was either deliberate or indiscriminate, and we're not going to charge the actual violences, which could very easily be incorporated under crimes against humanity. We're not saying you either charge war crimes or crimes against humanity. All we're saying in a state of armed conflict in order to determine whether there have been crimes committed, whether the mens rea of crimes against humanity doesn't matter, but the underlying offense has to be within in the framework of the laws of war. And the fact that the Prosecution now two months before the trial says, Oh, okay. If you want us to charge Hague violations, we will. With due respect, this is unconscionable. This indictment is five and a half years old. Surely, the Prosecution knows the difference between Hague law and Geneva law of violation. In every other case, the Prosecution has respected that distinction; in Galic, in Milosevic, in every case. And we now hear for the first time the argument, which is a categorical legal assertion: We don't need to prove occupation because it is not an element of the crime. What about the Prosecution's own pre-trial briefs which categorically state the requirements of Article 49 apply. So this is why we are left trying to understand how we can possibly go to trial with this indictment. Now, if I may just add, one of the issues is if the Prosecution had charged Hague law violations, you can be sure that we would be bringing both sides many expert witnesses, many direct witnesses, who are going to speak about what was the military intention on the ground, were Serbian forces using civilian buildings in order to launch attacks against Croatia, these type of questions, what was the technology available to General Gotovina, what --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard that?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: So this is a totally different case. This is one thing to say people were forcibly expelled. So that's why we cannot go to trial, if it is the case that we are -- that General Gotovina is going to be prosecuted for Hague law violations without being charged with those cases. There is no gap in the protection of humanitarian law. The crime of spreading terror against civilians is more than adequate for the job. The Hague law has more than enough provisions to protect civilians. The issue here is not that we're leaving victims without protection. The issue here is the accused has to be properly charged in accordance with customary law. The customary law cannot be re-written at the 11th hour. And that is why it is beyond the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to totally disregard Article 49 of the Geneva Convention, Article 86 of Protocol I, Rule 29 of the ICRC study, the Stakic judgement, and every other judgement. And one final point, if I may, the three cases cited by the Prosecution -- excuse me, Blagojevic, Stakic, and Brdjanin, this is my final remark, if you look at those cases the Prosecution has not charged shelling as an element of deportation in any of those cases. The Prosecution has charged that once Republika Srpska authorities controlled the territory in question, they, in an orderly and systematic fashion, deported people. That is the charge. The judgement itself only discusses shelling in the section on factual background. It is by way of factual background to establish a coercive context. If that is the theory that you create a coercive context through shelling, then you occupy territory and you deport people, then it may be factually relevant. But that is not what the Prosecution is doing in this case. They are saying the shelling itself was a modality of deportation, and that is why all of the precedents cited by the Prosecution are not in any way on point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I see that I -- at least I understand that Prosecutorial policy and the limits to Prosecutorial policy are to be considered perhaps as well. We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say to what Mr. Akhavan said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear you correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out if you had anything to add to what has been said by Mr. Akhavan, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have nothing to add. I fully agree with what Mr. Akhavan has said. I only wish to reply very briefly to the thesis put forward by my learned friend from the Prosecution when addressing the Tribunal. In my view, the Prosecutor has entered these proceedings with an erroneous thesis, and that is that if we were to say that this court was not -- did not have jurisdiction to try the perpetrators of the crimes which occurred after the end of Operation Storm, because we assert there was no armed conflict, in my view the Prosecutor then draws the erroneous conclusion that that would make those actions lawful. I wish to state quite clearly that the Prosecution does not by any means consider that the events which occurred at the end of Operation Storm, and we do know that there was burning of houses, that there was looting, that there were robberies, that there were murders, and in no way do we wish to deny that such unlawful acts occurred, but what we are trying to say, however, is that this Tribunal does not have jurisdiction to try those crimes because they occurred beyond the scope of an armed conflict; rather, it is the judiciary authorities of the Republic of Croatia which would have the authority to try those crimes. That is our argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just a few points very briefly in response to the additional submissions that we've heard from the Defence. First of all, the distinction that they seek to draw between Hague law violations and Geneva law violations, it is our position that that is an artificial and invalid distinction to make. Our position in this case is that the unlawful shelling was carried out as a means through which the deportation forcible transfer was effected in this case, and there is absolutely no limitation on the Prosecution's ability to proceed in this case on that basis. The definition of deportation which has been accepted by the Appeals Chamber in this case -- in -- before this Tribunal, itself recognises that deportation can be carried out through either expulsion or any other coercive act. Our case is in this particular factual scenario shelling was such a coercive action, which then facilitated the deportation. We point out also that there is one very clear example of Hague law violations under the Defence terminology being accepted as the basis on which a crimes against humanity charge was founded and that is of course the Galic case, where convictions based on inhumane acts as crimes against humanity were founded upon the shelling and sniping that was carried out in Sarajevo. And there's no reason in the case law of this Tribunal to limit such an approach in this particular case. In terms of the Defence point that -- on the colonisation argument, I think it's been clarified that obviously the Prosecution is not bringing a separate charge of colonisation under Article 49 of the Geneva Convention. The Defence now seek to say that if that is not the case, then the Prosecution is prohibited from using the evidence in relation to that matter in any way. We say that it's a perfectly valid approach that factual matters that in and of themselves are not charged as separate crimes can be considered as relevant evidentiary factors for assessing whether the elements of crimes have been met. There are many examples of that, Your Honours. For example, with the crime of genocide, it may be that particular acts like cultural genocide, burning of libraries, that kind of thing, would not in and of themselves amount to a crime, but that's nevertheless no barrier for not taking that into account as part of assessing the mens rea of the accused in that particular case for the crime of genocide. And there is no difference between that kind of a process and the way in which the indictment has been drafted in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Just one final point, Your Honours. We want to make it very clear that we reject the Defence contention that there is any kind of requirement of control over a territory or that the victims be in the hands of the opposite party to the conflict for displacement crimes under internal conflicts. We reject the Defence characterisation that the relevant IHL provisions themselves import such requirement. We have pointed out that Protocol II and Article 17 by its own terms are as broad as it could possibly be. It refers to anybody in the territory in which the armed conflict is taking place. And if -- Your Honours, if you look at the terms of the provision and the commentary as a whole, it's absolutely clear that there were not intended to be any limitations imported into that protection along the lines that the Defence have argued. Unless I can be of any further assistance, Your Honours, I will leave the matter with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. Would it be possible for me to briefly clarify a certain point at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it anything that you haven't clarified already, Mr. Akhavan?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, yes it is. It's a new argument which the Prosecution has raised in relation to Article 17 that I thought I should briefly address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long do you need to do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: It will take me just a few minutes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How few is few?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Just two minutes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, it's very intriguing that the Prosecution now argues for the application of the Article 17 of Protocol II, when in its written submissions it argues that it is not applicable. It argues that the restriction of the crime of forcible displacement to ordering, which is what Protocol II provides in Article 17, does not apply. Now, for the first time, we hear that Article 17 should apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Now, we just returned briefly to Judge Schomburg's statement. We hear that the Appeals Chamber does not require occupation. Here's what Judge Schomburg says: "Article 5 deportation must be "from an area under the actual control of one belligerent party to an area under the actual control of another."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You quoted that a little earlier in your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: What I would like to end on is the question of whether the Prosecution has discretion to charge a crime where it clearly fails to satisfy established jurisprudence, and I just want to end by quoting from the Tadic jurisdiction decision, which sets forth the standard for when the Prosecution should not have jurisdiction -- should not have discretion to make such charges. And this statement of the Tadic Appeals Chamber says that Rule 72 recognises that a matter as fundamental as jurisdiction "should not be kept for a decision at the end of the potentially lengthy, emotional, and expensive trial." And that "the higher interests of justice would not be served by a decision in favour of the accused after the latter would have undergone what would have to be branded as an unwarranted trial." Our submission is that the Prosecution has considerable discretion, but where the Prosecution, against the clear jurisprudence of this Tribunal, against its own settled practice, charges a crime that is manifestly at variance with customary law. It is violating the nullum crimen sine lege principle, and we respectfully submit that it would be unthinkable to go to trial on such a basis, especially at a time when the scarce resources of this Tribunal should certainly not be squandered on a charge that manifestly fails to satisfy customary law. I apologise, but thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber is grateful to the parties for their submissions. We will take into account what has been said by both sides. Can we move on to the next point. By a decision rendered yesterday, the Trial Chamber invited Mr. Separovic to answer. I see you nodding, Mr. Separovic. You have, I guess, seen the decision. Are you in a position to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The decision does indicate that you will be invited and be given an opportunity at this hearing to show a cause why the Trial Chamber should not act in terms of Rule 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, may I ask the Court a question before my colleague Mr. Separovic addresses the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I, of course, saw the Court's decision yesterday that was published, and my question to the Chamber is at this point would alter the Chamber's decision if General Gotovina decides not to call Mr. Separovic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your question is a little late, Mr. Kehoe. You have told us that you are likely to call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And given -- I also argue and discussed during our last hearing, Judge Moloto, the invaluable necessity that we -- that General Gotovina saw that Mr. Separovic continue to represent Mr. Markac. And I also addressed, Your Honour, to say that should we explore the possibility of some type of stipulated facts that we could agree to in some fashion concerning Mr. Separovic's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber is concerned that the trial starts and starts as soon as possible. Okay. I think what you are telling me should have been done a long time ago. It has not been done. Can we give Mr. Separovic to answer the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was simply putting it on the table --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- as a possibility to alleviate these concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take note of what you're said. Thank you very much. Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I received a decision yesterday, and I wish to thank you for allowing me to set out my reasons, if I understood you correctly, why I believe that my conduct to date has not been contrary to the interests of my client and has not been inappropriate. I wish to assure you that no further measures against me should be taken by Your Honours. You found that I had a conflict of interest and that I had personal interest and personal knowledge in this case. I wish to explain to Your Honours why I continued to assert that there is no conflict of interest, that I did not behave inappropriately in advocating my standpoint, and that I did not violate the rights of my client or fail to respect this Court. I have not been in contempt. In the Appeals Chamber decision, it is clearly stated that Separovic, as a necessary witness, is expected to withdraw from the case unless he can prove that General Markac will suffer as a result. And pursuant to Article 26 of the Code of Conduct, I stated that my client would suffer hardship were his counsel to withdraw at this stage of the proceedings. That is the first reason why I feel my behaviour has not been inappropriate. The second reason is my client's interest. He asked me, in spite of any potential conflict of interest, to remain his Defence counsel, because he knows very well that I was Minister of Justice. He knows what my role was in all of this; and in spite of all this, he asked me to stay on as his Defence counsel. In yesterday's decision by the Trial Chamber, there is a new element I may have misunderstood, but Article 14 of the code is mentioned and personal interests are mentioned. It would appear, based on this, that I have some kind of personal interest for wishing to remain in this case. I wish to assure you that I have no personal interest whatsoever, that the only interest is the interest of my client, unless I understand you to be saying that every member of the then-government is a potential member of the joint criminal enterprise. Were this the case, that every member of the government would be -- or of the cabinet would be a member of the joint criminal enterprise, this would then discredit me as Defence counsel. However, at this stage of the proceedings, it is premature to say that there even was a JCE, let alone that all the members of the cabinet were members of the JCE. My starting point is that there is a presumption of innocence and that I am presumed innocent until proved guilty, that I have never been under investigation. I have never been interviewed by the OTP, and so there is no personal interest and no inappropriate behaviour. The right to choose one's own counsel, according to Article 21, paragraph 4 of the Statute, overrides any theoretical possibility that I might be called as a witness in these proceedings. The third reason, I feel that my behaviour has not been inappropriate and that it has been in the interests of may client are the legal standards and precedents of this Tribunal, studying the legal standards, and I have put forward my arguments in this respect. I feel that there should be a balance between the interests of justice and the right to selection of counsel and that my withdrawal would create an imbalance at the expense of my client and that there should be a correct assessment of whether I really am a necessary witness. I am not a necessary witness. I do not have specific knowledge. I am not -- I was not an American Minister of Justice who can try people; mine was simply an administrative position in relation to the judicial system. Furthermore, there are the precedents of this Tribunal. I refer to IT-95-09-PT versus the accused Simic, where the late Judge May presided, and I do not notice any reference to this in the decision. Mr. Pisarevic, the lawyer, was a direct eye-witness of the events in the camp for which his client was charged. He was recognised in the courtroom by witnesses. Judge May concluded that Pisarevic was a necessary witness, that there was a conflict of interest, but the accused Simic made a statement which removed that in the light of Article 14 of the Code of Professional Conduct for Counsel. Your Honours, if Article 21 of the Statute states that all persons are equal before the ICTY, why would the accused Simic be more equal than my client, Mr. Markac? Why should counsel Pisarevic, in whose case a conflict of interest was established and who was recognised by witnesses as a necessary witness, was allowed to stay and his co-counsel was allowed to cross-examine those particular witnesses? That's reason number 4 why I believe my behaviour has not been inappropriate. I was simply putting forward the arguments I feel justify my position. The fourth and final argument is something that was conveyed to me from General Gotovina and published in the Croatian press, that they have decided I am not, after all, a necessary witness, and that this issue will not be raised again, that I will not be called. So I do not understand to this day the standpoint of the Defence counsel for General Gotovina, whether they feel that I should or should not be a necessary witness, and I appeal to Your Honours to put that question to them. I have acted honourably to the best of my knowledge in defending the interests of my client. I believe that my behaviour has not been inappropriate and contrary to the interests of my client. I am awaiting the decision of the Court. I will use my right to appeal, of course; but in line with Rule 46 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I ask Your Honours to issue a decision and General Markac's stating that General Markac's statement cannot have the same effect that Mr. Simic's statement had, and I will then withdraw but I will use my right to appeal. Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic, the Appeals Chamber has explained that one of the issues in the case against the three accused would be whether it would be the Minister of Defence or the Minister of Justice, which would be in charge -- would be responsible for the functioning of the military system. Would it be in the interest of your client or from the other accused where the accused were mainly related to the Ministry of Defence, to -- well, to blame another ministry rather than their own ministry for not functioning or -- well, whatever, for their involvement in the events or their involvement in not responding to the events?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think I understood you well I'm afraid, but let me nevertheless reply. The Ministry of Justice did not have any ability to affect the events the way that it is attributed to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Separovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case I did not understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you did not. And apart from that we not in a position here to introduce all kinds of facts that have been established either positively or negatively. My question is where it clearly appears from the indictment that the three accused in this case were functioning, I would say in the context, whether direct responsibility or not, but they're all people in military functions, and we all know that the military usually directly linked to the Ministry of Defence. Now, one of the core issues in this case -- or at least one of the issues would be whether it was the Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of Justice that would be responsible for the functioning of the military justice. My question was whether you would agree with me that the three accused, all linked to the Minister of Defence, that it could have an exculpatory effect if the blame could be shifted to another ministry; to say it was not we who were responsible, not the Ministry of Defence, not the military, rather, other people were responsible. Would you agree that it might assist them in their defence if they were heading for an acquittal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, certainly that it might. However, what I'm saying that the facts that need to be established are not the facts that I have exclusive knowledge of. I'm saying that my testimony would not greatly contribute to the interests of justice. This theoretical possibility that you are considering cannot have primacy over the interests of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're moving to Article 26 of the code, which says if you are a necessary witness you should not act unless certain circumstances. I'm focusing on Article 14, because if it might be in the interests of the accused to shift the blame to -- well, let's say not the Ministry of Defence, and if the Appeals Chamber has stated that one of the issues would be Ministry of Defence or Ministry of Justice, that you would not, by blaming others, that there would be an objective risk that you might blame one of the other ministries, perhaps even the one which is mentioned as a competitor and who is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But forgive me, why me? Forgive me, why me? Do you think that I am a potential suspect in the proceedings? I don't understand. I don't see why you think that I need to reply. Am I a member of a joint criminal enterprise? Am I seen as one? I don't see why I need to answer that question, why am I the necessary person who needs to say that. Your Honours, despite great efforts, I cannot understand that, except if you think that by mere fact that I was a Minister of Justice, I was a potential member of the JCE, which automatically then disqualifies me. It is only in this light that I can accept what you're saying; otherwise, I fully disagree with you because I do not think there was a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course, I understand that. That's another matter. No. The issue is your freedom to shift any blame as charged by the Prosecution from military defence circles to other circles where you played a prominent role in one of these other circles. That's the issue. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPAROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forgive me… I do understand, but no, not me… Nobody's going to shift blame; you saw that General Markac had already given a statement and had not shifted blame. And, second, your Honours, it would not be me but General Markac. Why do you think I would be the one to shift blame? I mean… I would, as far as his interest is concerned, but this has not been done, nor has anyone ever mentioned it. He made a statement, and it never occurred to him to say something to that effect. But if it did, he would be the one saying it, not me. That is why I don’t see why I, as his counsel, would need to testify about that or affect it in any way. I simply don’t understand.
